t.3.48.1: Then Jaṭāyu, who had been asleep, heard that cry. He quickly looked toward Rāvaṇa and saw Vaidehī.
t.3.48.2: Then that splendid best of birds, resembling a mountain peak and sharp of beak, perched upon a tree, spoke these auspicious words.
t.3.48.3: O Daśagrīva, I am the mighty king of vultures, Jaṭāyu by name, established in the ancient dharma and devoted to truth.
t.3.48.4: Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is king of the whole world, equal to great Indra and Varuṇa, and devoted to the welfare of all the worlds.
t.3.48.5: This illustrious, fair-hipped lady named Sītā, whom you wish to carry off from here, is the lawful wife of that lord of the world.
t.3.48.6: How can a king who stands firm in dharma lay hands on the wives of others? The wives of a king must be protected above all, O mighty one; turn back your base intent to violate another's wife.
t.3.48.7: A wise man should not do that for which another would censure him. Just as one's own wife must be protected from violation, so too must the wives of others.
t.3.48.8: O delight of the Paulastyas, whether it be a matter of wealth, of desire, or of dharma not found in the treatises, the learned make their decision by following the king.
t.3.48.9: The king is righteousness and pleasure, and the supreme treasury of riches; righteousness, and whatever is auspicious or sinful, proceeds with the king as its root.
t.3.48.10: O best of rākṣasas, how have you, wicked by nature and fickle as you are, attained sovereignty, like an evildoer gaining a celestial chariot?
t.3.48.12: When the mighty Rāma, whose soul is devoted to dharma, does you no wrong either in your realm or in your city, how can you wrong him?
t.3.48.11: Whatever lustful nature belongs to a person cannot be wiped away; for nobility does not long dwell in the abode of the wicked-souled.
t.3.48.13: If Khara, who was stationed in Janasthāna and had transgressed all bounds, was slain before on account of Śūrpaṇakhā by Rāma, whose deeds are accomplished without effort…
t.3.48.14: Tell me truly here: what offense has Rāma, the lord of the world, committed, that you would carry off his wife and go away?
t.3.48.16: Having tied a venomous serpent in the hem of your garment, you do not realize it; nor do you see the noose of Death fastened around your neck.
t.3.48.15: Release Vaidehī at once, lest he burn you with his terrible, fire-like gaze, as Indra's thunderbolt burned Vṛtra.
t.3.48.17: O gentle one, that burden should be borne which does not crush a man; that food should be eaten which is digested and causes no illness.
t.3.48.18: Having done which, there would be neither dharma, nor fame, nor glory on earth, but only weariness of the body, who would undertake such a deed?
t.3.48.19: O Rāvaṇa, sixty thousand years have passed since I was born, while I have duly governed the kingdom inherited from my father and forefathers.
t.3.48.20: I am old, while you are young, armed with a bow, mounted on a chariot, clad in armor and furnished with arrows; even so, having seized Vaidehī, you shall not go away unharmed.
t.3.48.21: You are not able to carry off Vaidehī by force while I look on, just as one cannot overthrow the firm revelation of the Veda with arguments joined to logic.
t.3.48.22: Fight, if you are a hero! Stand still for a moment, Rāvaṇa, and you will lie slain upon the ground, just as Khara did before.
t.3.48.23: Rāma, clad in bark garments, by whom Daityas and Dānavas have again and again been slain in combat, will before long kill you in battle.
t.3.48.25: While I am alive, you shall surely not carry off this lovely Sītā, the lotus-petal-eyed, the beloved queen of Rāma.
t.3.48.24: What indeed can I do, now that the two sons of the king have gone far away? You are fleeing swiftly, O vile one, afraid of those two; of that there is no doubt.
t.3.48.27: Stop, stop, ten-necked Rāvaṇa, and watch for a moment, O night-roamer: I shall give you the hospitality of battle as far as my life allows, and I would fell you from your excellent chariot like a fruit from its stalk.
t.3.48.26: But I must surely do what is dear to that great-souled Rāma, and likewise to Daśaratha, even at the cost of my own life.
